meta.title: Multi-agent Orchestration
meta.thesis: Multi-agent Orchestration becomes practical when you can map it to a decision, a workflow, and a validation check.

mentalMap.title: Multi-agent Orchestration: mental map
mentalMap.caption: Use multi-agent orchestration only when specialization, breadth, or independent checking beats coordination cost.
mentalMap.oneLineThesis: A multi-agent system is an organizational design: topology, delegation packets, shared state, merge rules, and evaluation matter more than agent count.

modules.title: Use teams for breadth, not theater
modules.sub: More agents help only when the task has real substructure.
modules.summary: A team should beat a single agent on a named axis.
objectives: Explain when multi-agent systems are useful.

blocks.title: Agent count is not intelligence by itself

spans.text: Problem anchor: a lesson-quality review must check schema, source grounding, pedagogy, and code examples across many files. Separate workers can inspect disjoint slices or specialize in citations versus schema. A second “creative thinker” with no ownership adds little.

Multi-agent orchestration is valuable for breadth, specialization, independent verification, or context isolation. It is harmful when workers repeat each other, inherit a bad plan, or produce unsupported summaries.
Write the sentence “Worker B exists because...” and include the metric it should improve.

blocks.analogy: A team is useful when people own different jobs, not when five people hold the same clipboard.

spans.text: A coordinator assigns one worker to schema/render validation and another to source-grounding review. Each returns findings with file paths, evidence, and confidence. The coordinator merges conflicts and decides fixes.
The team is justified because the checks are independent and can run in parallel. A vague brainstorming swarm would not be justified.

items.text: Measure quality, latency, and cost against baseline.

blocks.title: Team fit
blocks.prompt: What is the best reason to add a second agent?

options.text: It owns an independent subtask or critique that measurably improves the outcome.
It lets every worker use production admin tools.

blocks.explanation: Topology should serve the task, not the other way around.

modules.title: Topology assigns ownership and state
modules.sub: Supervisor-worker, debate, swarm, and pipeline patterns behave differently.
objectives: Compare supervisor-worker, pipeline, debate, and blackboard patterns.
Choose a topology by task shape.

blocks.title: The topology is the operating model

spans.text: A supervisor-worker team centralizes planning and synthesis. A pipeline gives each stage one owner. A debate or critic loop compares candidate answers. A blackboard lets workers contribute to shared state while a controller arbitrates.
Shared state should be intentional: findings, citations, unresolved questions, and artifacts. Private scratchpads should not become unreviewed evidence.
If no one owns final synthesis, the system will merge by vibes.

blocks.analogy: Topology is the org chart and meeting protocol for agents.

blocks.title: Topology fit
blocks.prompt: Which topology fits independent file audits best?

options.text: An unbounded swarm with no coordinator.
Supervisor-worker with disjoint file ownership and merge review.
A single critic that never sees files.

blocks.explanation: Independent audits need clear work packets and final merge.

modules.title: Delegation packets constrain workers
modules.sub: A worker needs scope, tools, output schema, and stop rules.
modules.summary: The packet is the API between coordinator and worker.
objectives: Write a worker brief with ownership and evidence rules.
Limit tools and context per worker.

blocks.title: Delegation is not “go think about this”

spans.text: A good packet states the task, files or sources owned, allowed tools, forbidden actions, expected output schema, evidence requirements, confidence labels, and stop conditions.

Workers should know they are not alone in the codebase and must not revert unrelated changes. For safety, tool access should match the packet: a citation reviewer does not need production write tools.
If the coordinator cannot verify a worker result from the returned evidence, the packet is too vague.

blocks.analogy: Delegation packets are job tickets with acceptance criteria.

spans.text: Task: inspect three RAG lessons for source support. Scope: only listed files. Tools: read files, run validator. Output: findings with file path, block ID, unsupported claim, source evidence, severity. Stop: return after all files or blocker.
The worker is not asked for a broad opinion. It returns reviewable evidence the coordinator can merge.

blocks.title: Delegation quality
blocks.prompt: What makes a worker result hard to use?

options.text: It includes exact paths and source citations.
It gives a confident summary without evidence, scope, or file references.
It states uncertainty on ambiguous findings.

blocks.explanation: The coordinator needs verifiable outputs, not ungrounded confidence.

modules.title: Merge evidence before synthesis
modules.sub: The coordinator must dedupe, resolve conflicts, and check support.
objectives: Preserve provenance into the final answer.

blocks.title: The coordinator is an editor with a ledger

spans.text: Workers may duplicate effort, disagree, miss citations, or overstate confidence. The coordinator should merge by evidence: source, trace, metric, or test result. Unsupported claims become follow-up tasks or caveats.
Conflict handling should be explicit. If one worker says a file validates and another reports render failure, the coordinator runs or requests the decisive check.
Every final claim should trace back to a worker finding, tool result, or source.

blocks.title: Merge worker findings with evidence checks
blocks.explanation: The toy merge deduplicates identical claims and sends low-confidence findings to follow-up instead of treating every worker output as final.

predictThenReveal.prompt: Before reading the answer, predict what happens to the MCP policy finding.
predictThenReveal.answer: It is marked `needs_follow_up` because confidence is below 0.8, even though it includes some evidence.

blocks.title: Merge discipline
blocks.prompt: How should a coordinator treat a worker claim without evidence?

options.text: Include it because workers are always reliable.
Request evidence, verify independently, or exclude it from synthesis.
Hide it in the final answer without attribution.

blocks.explanation: Multi-agent systems still need grounded evidence.

modules.title: Evaluate topology against a single-agent baseline
modules.sub: Teams must earn their added cost and risk.
modules.summary: The final question is whether the topology improves the product.
objectives: Compare topology variants on same tasks.
Track token, tool, and latency budgets.

blocks.title: The baseline keeps the team honest

spans.text: Run the same tasks with one agent, supervisor-worker, critic loop, and deterministic workflow where possible. Compare recall, correctness, citations, tool count, cost, latency, and human review needs.
Safety evaluation must cover each agent’s permissions and communication path. A research worker should not gain write access because the coordinator has it.
If the multi-agent version costs 3x and improves nothing measurable, remove the team.

blocks.title: Verify AI output from a multi-agent system

spans.text: Review the topology and final answer together.

items.text: Each worker had disjoint scope, allowed tools, and output schema.
Findings include evidence, confidence, and unresolved questions.
The coordinator deduped results and resolved conflicts before final synthesis.
Tool permissions were scoped per worker, not inherited broadly.
Evaluation compares quality, latency, cost, and safety against a single-agent baseline.

blocks.title: Baseline decision
blocks.prompt: A multi-agent team costs twice as much and produces the same grounded answers as one agent. What should you do?

options.text: Keep the team because more agents are always more advanced.
Prefer the simpler single-agent or deterministic workflow unless another measured benefit exists.

blocks.explanation: Added orchestration must earn its complexity.

agent.label: Agent
agent.laymanDefinition: A software loop that plans, observes results, and may use tools to pursue a goal.
agent.technicalNote: Agent designs need explicit loop boundaries, stop conditions, permissions, state contracts, and evaluation surfaces before autonomy is useful.

tool.label: Tool
tool.laymanDefinition: An external capability the model can request, such as search, code execution, retrieval, or a business API.
tool.technicalNote: Tools require schemas, authorization, error handling, audit logs, and tests because natural-language intent is not execution permission.

state.label: State
state.laymanDefinition: The working information carried between steps of an agent workflow.
state.technicalNote: State should separate durable facts, transient scratch work, approvals, tool results, and failure metadata so retries and handoffs remain understandable.

memory.label: Memory
memory.laymanDefinition: Information saved across turns or sessions for future use.
memory.technicalNote: Agent memory needs scope, freshness, deletion, privacy controls, and evaluation so saved context helps rather than silently steering behavior.

mcp.label: MCP
mcp.laymanDefinition: A protocol for exposing tools and context to models and agent clients.
mcp.technicalNote: MCP-style integrations still need capability design, trust boundaries, lifecycle handling, and authorization around each exposed server.

sandbox.label: Sandbox
sandbox.laymanDefinition: An isolated environment that limits what agent actions can reach or change.
sandbox.technicalNote: Sandboxing should constrain files, network, processes, credentials, browser sessions, time, and side effects according to the task risk.

questions.q: What value does the second agent create that one well-tooled agent cannot?
questions.why: Coordination consumes tokens, time, and safety surface; it must earn its keep.
questions.rot: Add agents only when ownership, parallelism, or independent critique improves measured outcomes.
